stem: Let f(x) = √x. Using the limit definition of the derivative, evaluate f′(9) = lim(h→0) [√(9 + h) − 3] / h.

rationales.A: This limit is the definition of f′(9) for f(x) = √x, since f(9 + h) − f(9) = √(9 + h) − 3. Because f′(x) = 1/(2√x), f′(9) = 1/(2·3) = 1/6.
rationales.B: 1/3 comes from using the derivative of √x as 1/√x, forgetting the factor 1/2. The correct derivative is 1/(2√x), so the limit is 1/(2·3) = 1/6.
rationales.C: 6 comes from inverting the derivative, 2√9 = 6. The derivative of √x at 9 is 1/(2√9) = 1/6, not its reciprocal.
rationales.D: Substituting h = 0 gives 0/0, which is indeterminate rather than 0. The limit is the derivative of √x at x = 9, namely 1/6.

title: Limit as a derivative

stem: If f(x) = 3/x², which of the following is f′(x)?

rationales.A: This gets the new exponent −3 right but keeps the coefficient 3 (with a negative sign) instead of multiplying 3 by the exponent −2. The power rule gives 3(−2)x⁻³ = −6/x³.
rationales.B: This loses the negative sign from the exponent −2. The power rule gives 3(−2)x⁻³ = −6/x³.
rationales.D: This adds 1 to the exponent (−2 + 1 = −1) instead of subtracting 1. The new exponent is −3, so f′(x) = −6/x³.

title: Power rule with negative exponent

stem: If f(x) = 4e^x − 2cos x, what is f′(π/2)?

rationales.A: This treats e^x like a power function, using n·x^(n−1) with x as the multiplier: 4·(π/2)·e^(π/2 − 1). The power rule needs a variable base and a constant exponent; the derivative of e^x is e^x, so the first term is 4e^(π/2).
rationales.B: This uses (cos x)′ = sin x instead of −sin x. The correct derivative is 4e^x − 2(−sin x) = 4e^x + 2sin x, giving 4e^(π/2) + 2.
rationales.D: This uses (cos x)′ = −cos x, so the cosine term becomes +2cos(π/2) = 0. The derivative of cos x is −sin x, so that term contributes +2sin(π/2) = 2 and f′(π/2) = 4e^(π/2) + 2.

title: Derivative of e^x and cos x
